whyThisMatters: Most incidents do not start with hacking. They start with someone opening the wrong message. Today you will practise noticing the small details that give a fake away, whatever your role.
rememberThis: One habit: pause for ten seconds before you click or tap. Stop, Verify through a channel you already trust (a known phone number or a saved bookmark), then Report anything suspicious to IT.

discussionPrompts: Ask which detail people noticed first: the sender domain, the Reply-To, the attachment type or the link? Would they check the same thing on their phone?
For the link card, ask how many people hover over (or press and hold) a link before they click. What makes that hard when you are busy?
Ask if anyone has seen a text, a pop-up or a flood of approval requests like the last three cards. What did they do?
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: People often trust a message because it fits an ongoing thread or has a padlock and a familiar name. Real and fake look almost identical. Build the habit of checking the exact sender domain, the real link destination and the file type, then Stop, Verify, Report.

items.title: Real vs Fake Job Offer Email
items.whatIsWrong: Both emails say "HR Recruitment" and look the same. The real sender is hr@acmecorp.com. The fake sender is hr@acmecorp.co: the last letter of the domain is missing. The fake also has a Reply-To address on a different domain (mailbox-hr.net), so your reply would go to a stranger. The fake's attachment is an .html file you are asked to open and sign in to, while the real one is a PDF.
items.whyItsSuspicious: The display name ("HR Recruitment") is just text anyone can type. Only the domain after the @ tells you who really sent it, and it must match exactly: acmecorp.com, not acmecorp.co. Mail systems can also flag a sender that fails SPF or DKIM checks, which is the mail server saying "this sender cannot prove it owns this domain", but you cannot count on that warning being shown. An unexpected .html attachment that asks you to sign in is a way to steal your password. Stop: do not open it or reply. Verify: call HR on a number you already know. Report: send it to IT. That is Stop-Verify-Report.

items.title: Real vs Fake Bank-Detail Change Email
items.whatIsWrong: Both emails look like part of the same supplier payment thread, and neither shouts. The real one confirms the 28 Nov payment and says to follow the normal approval chain and call a known number for any bank change. The fake sender is finance@acme-corp.com (a hyphen added). It quietly asks you to pay a new account, skip the ticket, and reply instead of calling because "phones are down". It also mentions a 15:00 cut-off.
items.whyItsSuspicious: A familiar thread and a calm tone do not make a message safe. Attackers join real conversations so the request feels normal. Two tells matter: the sender domain is not exactly acmecorp.com, and the message asks you to skip a control (approval or call-back). A bank-detail change should always be confirmed by phone. Stop: do not pay or reply. Verify: call the supplier on a number already in your records. Report: tell Finance and IT. That is Stop-Verify-Report.

items.title: Real vs Fake Payslip Email
items.whatIsWrong: Both emails are from hr-payroll@acmecorp.com and both say "Hi Sam". The real one sends Payslip_Feb2025_SamLee.pdf and Team_Schedule_Feb-Apr.xlsx, as you requested. The fake one sends Payslip_Mar2025_SamLee.html (a web page, not a document) and Team_Schedule_Mar-May.zip, and says to sign in to view the payslip. Nobody asked for these, and the real payslip is in the HR portal.
items.whyItsSuspicious: A file's ending shows what it really is. A payslip should be a PDF. An .html file opens a fake login page in your browser, and a .zip, .iso or .html can also hide programs. A sender address that looks right is not proof, because real accounts can be hacked. Ask: did I expect this, and does the file type fit? Stop: do not open it. Verify: check your payslip in the HR portal using your own bookmark. Report: send the email to IT. That is Stop-Verify-Report.

items.title: Real vs Fake Schedule Confirmation Email
items.whatIsWrong: The link text looks the same in both emails: https://portal.acmecorp.com/staff/schedule-confirm. In the fake, hovering (or pressing and holding on a phone) shows the real destination: https://portal.acmecorp.com.staff-verify.net/schedule-confirm?id=42. The owner of a web address is the part just before the first single slash, so the registrable domain here is staff-verify.net. "portal.acmecorp.com" is only a prefix added in front. The fake page even shows an HTTPS padlock.
items.whyItsSuspicious: The text of a link can say anything. Words before the real domain are just decoration. A padlock only means the connection is encrypted, not that the site is honest: criminals get padlocks too. Stop: hover or press and hold before you click. Verify: open the portal from your own bookmark. Report: send the email to IT if the preview does not match. That is Stop-Verify-Report.

items.title: Real vs Fake Staff Portal Login
items.whatIsWrong: The fake page's address bar reads "portal.acrnecorp.com". The letters "r" and "n" side by side look like an "m", so it passes for acmecorp at a glance. The real address is "portal.acmecorp.com". Both show a padlock, and the design, logo and wording are identical.
items.whyItsSuspicious: A page can be copied perfectly, but its address cannot be the real one. The padlock only means the connection is encrypted, and attackers get padlocks for their own domains. Read the address letter by letter, or better, reach login pages from a bookmark rather than a link in a message. Stop: do not type your password. Verify: open the portal from your own bookmark. Report: send the link to IT, and change your password at once if you already typed it. That is Stop-Verify-Report.

items.title: Fake Delivery Text Message
items.whatIsWrong: A text from "FastShip Delivery" says: "Your parcel is on hold: a 1.99 redelivery fee is due. Pay within 24 hours to avoid return: fastship.delivery-fee.co/p/4x9". It begins with a courier name, but the link's real domain is delivery-fee.co, not the courier's own site. You were not expecting a parcel, and the small fee makes it feel harmless.
items.whyItsSuspicious: This is smishing: phishing by text message. The name at the top is easy to fake. Look at the registrable domain in the link, the part just before the first slash: here it is delivery-fee.co, and "fastship" is only a prefix. A small payment request is a way to collect your card details. Phones hide detail, so it is easier to fall for. Stop: do not tap the link. Verify: open the courier's real app or website, typed in yourself. Report: forward the text to your IT team or mobile provider, then delete it. That is Stop-Verify-Report.

items.title: Fake IT Support Pop-Up
items.whatIsWrong: A box titled "Windows Security — Session Verification" says "Your session must be verified to finish a security update. Re-enter your password to continue", with a VERIFY button. It looks calm and shows a plausible IT Service Desk reference number. It appeared while you were working, and you had not asked for anything.
items.whyItsSuspicious: Real system and IT tools do not ask for your password in a pop-up. A ticket number and polite wording are easy to add. This box is a trick to steal your login. The tell: you started nothing that needs a password. Stop: close it and type nothing. Verify: contact the IT helpdesk through the number or ticket system you normally use. Report: tell IT, and on a shared computer warn the next user. That is Stop-Verify-Report.

items.title: Repeated Login Approval Requests
items.whatIsWrong: Your phone shows "Approve sign-in?" requests for Acme Mail and Acme VPN, arriving every few minutes over half an hour, from Lagos, NG, a place you are not in. You did not start any of them. MFA (multi-factor authentication) is the extra approval step after your password, such as a code or an Approve button.
items.whyItsSuspicious: Someone already has your password and hopes you will tap Approve to make the requests stop, or by mistake. This is called MFA fatigue. A slow drip is easier to miss than a flood. An approval you did not start is always a warning, even if only one arrives. Stop: tap Deny, never Approve. Verify: change your password from a device you trust. Report: tell the IT helpdesk right away. That is Stop-Verify-Report.
